analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its companion reconciliation law in full.
analysis.headline: All 48 Republican sponsors and cosponsors backed full repeal of the Affordable Care Act, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 — the two laws together that created the ACA's coverage expansions, insurance rules, Medicare drug discounts, tax surcharges on high earners, and the switch of federal student lending from banks to the Education Department. Everything the ACA changed would snap back to pre-2010 law six months after the bill was signed. The Senate read it twice and placed it on the calendar, and no vote ever happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households, who would stop paying the ACA's Medicare payroll surtax and the 3.8% tax on investment income; brand-name drug makers, who would no longer have to cover half the cost of seniors' Medicare drug coverage in the coverage gap; private student lenders, who would regain the subsidized federally guaranteed loan business that the 2010 reconciliation law ended; and health insurers, which would be freed from guaranteed-issue and community-rating rules, though they would also lose the subsidy-funded customers the ACA brought them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, drug makers, student lenders

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act entirely and restores the laws as they stood before 2010, effective 180 days after enactment [S2][S3].

Because the ACA's tax surcharges apply mainly to high earners and investment income, full repeal is a large tax cut concentrated at the top of the income scale (the taxes being repealed are part of the ACA the bill erases) [S2][S3].

The subjects include government lending, higher education, and student aid because the 2010 reconciliation law ended federally subsidized private student lending and moved loans to direct federal lending; restoring pre-2010 law returns that business to private lenders [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People who gained coverage or lower premiums through the ACA's Medicaid expansion and subsidized marketplace plans; people with pre-existing conditions, who would again face denial or surcharges under restored pre-2010 underwriting; seniors, who would again pay full price in the Medicare drug coverage gap; and students, who would borrow through bank intermediaries taking a federal subsidy on the same loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA enrollees, preexisting-condition patients, seniors, students

drawbacks.text: Repeal strips the insurance rules — guaranteed issue, community rating, bans on lifetime limits — that the ACA imposed, so the pre-2010 practice of denying or surcharging people with pre-existing conditions would return [S2][S3].

The ACA's premium subsidies and Medicaid expansion, which the bill repeals with no replacement, paid most of the cost of coverage for lower- and middle-income enrollees; those subsidies end 180 days after enactment [S2][S3].

The bill would raise the federal deficit by removing the ACA's dedicated taxes and spending offsets while the repeal itself is scored for pay-as-you-go purposes, an honest supporter acknowledges the coverage losses come with no transition plan or replacement framework in the bill text [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow narrowly — a large tax cut for high earners, restored profits for drug makers and private student lenders, and freedom from insurance rules for insurers — while the costs fall broadly on people who rely on ACA coverage, protections, and Medicare drug discounts. There is no replacement mechanism anywhere in the bill text; it is a clean repeal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, and no vote was ever scheduled before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the ObamaCare Repeal Act on February 2, 2015, with 47 Republican cosponsors, including Majority Leader Mitch McConnell [S1][S3][S4].
The bill would repeal the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 entirely, restoring pre-2010 law 180 days after enactment [S2][S3].
On February 3, 2015 the Senate read the bill a second time and placed it on the calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 11 [S5][S3].
No further action was ever taken; the bill remained on the calendar without a vote, hearing, or committee referral until the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on ACA coverage, protections, subsidies, and Medicare drug discounts are better off, because the repeal never advanced. High earners kept paying the ACA surtaxes, and drug makers and private student lenders kept operating under ACA-era rules and taxes rather than regaining repealed-away advantages.

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill in the Senate on February 2, 2015

for.name: 47 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making 48 Republican sponsors in total

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal, but as Majority Leader never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote; the bill sat on the calendar for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 48 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat joined; the bill never reached a roll-call vote, so the only recorded positions are the all-Republican sponsorship and the absence of any floor action.

industries.note: The 2010 reconciliation law ended federally guaranteed lending through private banks in favor of direct federal loans; full repeal restores the pre-2010 system in which private lenders originate student loans with a federal subsidy. Students would pay the middleman's cut on the same borrowing.
Repeal removes the ACA requirement that brand-name manufacturers cover 50% of seniors' drug costs in the Medicare coverage gap, shifting that cost back to beneficiaries.

Insurers would lose the ACA's subsidy-funded marketplace customers and Medicaid expansion business, but regain the ability to deny or surcharge people with pre-existing conditions and to sell skimpier plans.
Repeal eliminates the ACA's additional Medicare payroll tax and its 3.8% net investment income tax, which fall mainly on high earners, funded by coverage and benefit reductions that fall on others.
